title: Design Circular Deque
description: Design a fixed-capacity deque supporting O(1) insertion and removal at both ends, using a circular array with a head index and count.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a MyCircularDeque class with a fixed capacity k, supporting insertFront(value), insertLast(value), deleteFront(), deleteLast() (each returning true on success, false if the deque is full or empty respectively), getFront(), getRear() (both returning -1 if empty), isEmpty(), and isFull().

blocks.caption: A fixed array with a moving head index and a count supports insertion and removal from both ends.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Constructor","k (fixed maximum capacity)"],["insertFront / insertLast","Insert at the front / rear; false if already full"],["deleteFront / deleteLast","Remove from the front / rear; false if already empty"],["getFront / getRear","Return the front / rear value, or -1 if empty"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

A fixed-capacity structure supporting O(1) insertion and removal at BOTH ends is the circular buffer pattern extended in two directions: a "head" index moves backward for front insertions and forward for front deletions, while the "tail" position is always computed from head and count, needing no separate tracked variable.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Directly extends Design Circular Queue (front-only removal, rear-only insertion) by allowing insertion and removal at BOTH ends, which is exactly the queue-versus-deque distinction.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a circular row of k parking spots. Cars can park or leave from either end of the occupied stretch, and the row wraps around, so a car "beyond" the last spot actually wraps back to spot 0. A head pointer marks where the front car currently is, and the count of occupied spots (rather than a separate tail pointer) determines where the rear car is.

blocks.caption: Both ends of the deque can grow or shrink, wrapping around the fixed-size ring.

items: insertFront moves head one step BACKWARD (wrapping with modulo) before writing the new value there.
insertLast writes at position (head + count) mod capacity, since that is exactly one past the current rear.
deleteFront moves head one step FORWARD; deleteLast simply decrements count, since the old rear slot does not need to be cleared, only excluded from the logical range.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
MyCircularDeque(3), then insertLast(1), insertLast(2), insertFront(3), insertFront(4), getRear(), isFull(), deleteLast(), insertFront(4), getFront().

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Every result matches the official LeetCode example exactly: true, true, true, false, 2, true, true, true, 4.
5. How Should We Think?

A simple approach uses a built-in doubly linked list or deque data structure, which already supports O(1) insertion and removal at both ends. This is correct and simple but relies on a general-purpose structure rather than demonstrating the underlying circular-buffer mechanics.

Implementing it directly with a fixed array, a head index, and a count demonstrates the same O(1) guarantees without any dynamic allocation: front operations move the head pointer (with modulo wraparound), rear operations use the derived tail position (head + count) mod capacity, and capacity/emptiness checks are simple comparisons against count.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a built-in doubly-linked-list-backed deque, checking capacity before each insertion.

8. Optimize the Solution

Implement the deque directly with a fixed-size array, a head index, and a count. insertFront decrements head (with modulo wraparound) before writing; insertLast writes at the derived tail position; deleteFront increments head; deleteLast simply decrements count. getFront reads data[head], and getRear reads the derived tail position.

items: insertFront: head = (head - 1 + capacity) % capacity, then write data[head].
insertLast: tail = (head + count) % capacity, then write data[tail].
deleteFront: head = (head + 1) % capacity. deleteLast: just count--, no write needed.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A circular buffer supports O(1) insertion and removal at BOTH ends by tracking just a head index and a count, deriving the tail position from them.
Front insertion moves the head BACKWARD (with modulo wraparound); rear deletion needs no index movement at all, just a count decrement.
This exact pattern generalizes Design Circular Queue to full deque functionality with only a few additional lines.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Design Circular Deque is solved with a fixed-size array, a head index, and a count, deriving the tail position as (head + count) mod capacity. Front operations move the head index with modulo wraparound, while rear operations only need the derived tail position, giving O(1) time for every operation with no dynamic memory allocation.
